title: Chinmaya Mission's 75th Anniversary: How Atlanta's Diaspora Chanted the Gita Together
excerpt: More than 2,000 devotees gathered in Suwanee, Georgia, for an evening of mass Gita chanting, music and dance as part of the movement's year-long 75th anniversary commemoration.
body:
• Chinmaya Mission Atlanta and Chinmaya Mission Alpharetta jointly hosted the Chinmaya Amrit Mahotsav on April 19, 2026, at North Gwinnett High School in Suwanee, Georgia, marking 75 years of the Chinmaya movement.
  • More than 2,000 devotees, students, youth and community leaders attended an evening built around the mass chanting of Chapter 15 of the Bhagavad Gita, plus music, dance and discourses.
  • The celebration was part of a year-long global commemoration that included a Guinness World Records-certified mass online chanting on May 9, 2026, with 8,277 verified participants.
  • The Atlanta-area centers have served the community for 25 years, with more than 1,000 children attending weekly classes across Riverdale, Norcross, Alpharetta and Marietta.

An Evening of Chanting in Suwanee

On April 19, 2026, Chinmaya Mission Atlanta and Chinmaya Mission Alpharetta jointly hosted the Chinmaya Amrit Mahotsav at North Gwinnett High School in Suwanee, Georgia, commemorating 75 years of the Chinmaya movement's spiritual and educational legacy. More than 2,000 devotees, students, youth, community leaders and members of the public filled the venue for an evening-long celebration honoring the life and vision of Swami Chinmayananda.

The program centered on the mass chanting of Chapter 15 of the Bhagavad Gita, the Purushottama Yoga, led in three rounds by children and representatives from Chinmaya Mission Atlanta, the Swami Ganapati Satchidananda Gita Foundation and Chinmaya Mission Alpharetta. Organizers said the collective recitation by more than 2,000 participants created a meditative and uplifting atmosphere, according to reporting by Khabar and India Tribune.

The evening also featured Gita Panchamrit recitations, music and dance performances and spiritual discourses. A Kuchipudi presentation interpreted the essence of Chapter 15, and dance segments rendered the Gita's meditation verses in Bharatanatyam, Kuchipudi and Odissi, with compositions set by Subhashini Krishnamurthy and Sujatha Raburn. Students, teachers, parents and volunteers from both centers had spent months preparing under the guidance of Brahmacharini Jyoti Chaitanya and Acharyas Dr. G.V. Raghu, Geetha Raghu, Siva Velu and Sushma Siva.

Seventy-Five Years Since Pune

The milestone traces back to 1951, when Swami Chinmayananda began his first Bhagavad Gita Jnana Yagna in Pune, a movement that made the sacred text accessible as a practical guide for modern life. The year-long global commemoration, Chinmaya Amrit Mahotsav, honors 75 years of that legacy across spirituality, education, culture and community service.

One of its flagship events took place on May 9, 2026, when Chinmaya Gita Samarpanam brought together devotees worldwide for a simultaneous online chanting of Chapter 15. Guinness World Records certified the event with 8,277 verified participants chanting together on Cisco Webex, surpassing the previous benchmark of 5,188 and setting the record for the most people chanting online simultaneously.

"When thousands chant together with one heart and one intention, it becomes a powerful prayer for the welfare of the entire world — Lokah Samasthah Sukhino Bhavantu."

— Swami Swaroopananda, Global Head, Chinmaya Mission

Atlanta's Quarter-Century of the Mission

For the local community, the celebration also marked 25 years of Chinmaya Mission's presence in Atlanta. More than 1,000 children now attend weekly classes across centers in Riverdale, Norcross, Alpharetta and Marietta, a measure of how deeply the movement has rooted itself in the diaspora's second and third generations.

The Suwanee program opened with a dance presentation by Bala Vihar teachers honoring the Guru Paduka, followed by the Indian and American national anthems, exhibits on the Mission's history, cultural displays and a bookstore. Attendees received Gita Panchamrit booklets and refreshments at the close of the evening. The event, as the diaspora papers covering it noted, was less a commemoration than a demonstration: a 75-year-old movement still drawing thousands of young American Hindus to chant an ancient text together, out loud, in one hall.
